clue.text: Cake and stiff drink fed to cold animal

indicators.note: Whatever is fed to something ends up inside it, so the spirit is swallowed by the pieces on either side rather than standing next to them.

parts.note: c is the standard abbreviation for cold, the letter on the tap
rum is a strong spirit, the stiff drink of the sailor's tot
a pet is an animal kept at home

explanation.walkthrough: The surface lays out a tea table, so 'cold animal' reads as a shivering creature. It is two separate pieces of wordplay that happen to sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Cake -> CRUMPET: a crumpet is a soft griddle cake, toasted and buttered for tea, so the general word covers it as a type.

clue.text: Male rugby player initially doubled in value?

indicators.note: A word's initial is the letter it starts with, so only that leading character is touched and the rest stays put.
Read as a Roman numeral the letter is worth fifty, and twice fifty has a single-letter numeral of its own.

parts.note: a lock is a second-row forward, the tall one who packs down behind the front row
that leading L is fifty in Roman numerals, and a hundred is written as one letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubled in value' sounds like money, and the surface invites you to price a player. The sum is arithmetic done on a Roman numeral instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Male -> COCK: the male of the domestic fowl is a cock, so the bare adjective stands as the noun naming a bird by its sex.

clue.text: Expert breaking suspect exposed bursar's rackets

indicators.note: Something that breaks in forces its way inside, splitting the letters apart to make room for itself.
Letters you cannot trust will not stay in the order they were handed to you.
A word left exposed has had its covering letters stripped off, leaving only the middle on show.

parts.note: the four letters left in the middle once the outer pair of that word goes
a pro is a professional, expert enough to be paid for it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an interrogation, so 'rackets' reads as criminal schemes. The definition wants the other sense of the word entirely: plain noise.
explanation.definitionFit: rackets -> UPROARS: a racket is a din or loud disturbance, and the plural agrees, so this is an everyday synonym in its noise sense.

clue.text: Here we find Basil and Coot asleep occasionally, having retired

indicators.note: Something done occasionally happens every so often rather than every time, so you take every second letter and leave the rest.
A word that has retired has gone back the way it came, so the letters are read from the far end.

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of those two words, in that order

explanation.walkthrough: Two capital letters that look like two men: Basil is the herb, not Fawlty, and Coot is the setter signing his own clue and lending it letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Here we find Basil -> PESTO: basil leaves are the main ingredient of the sauce, so the clue points at where you would meet the herb.

clue.text: City suffering torn parts excessively

indicators.note: A place suffering is a place in a bad way, and letters in a bad way do not stay in the order given.
To part is to come away from what you were joined to, so the letters separate before they are put back together.

parts.note: four letters handed over exactly as printed
too much is more than enough, so this is the everyday word for excessively

explanation.walkthrough: 'Torn' reads as the instruction to tear the letters up. It is the fodder, and the words on either side of it are what do the tearing.
explanation.definitionFit: City -> TORONTO: Toronto is the largest city in Canada, so the bare word defines it by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: Oil producer's area of operation? Hour away east

indicators.note: A piece sent away is taken out, so the letter named just before it never reaches the finished word.

parts.note: a theatre of operations is the whole region a campaign is fought over, and the question mark nods at the surgical sort too
h is the standard abbreviation for hour
e is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.walkthrough: The oil comes from an Australian shrub of the myrtle family, nothing to do with the tea in your cup: only the name overlaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil producer -> TEA TREE: the crushed leaves of the shrub yield tea tree oil, so the plant is named for the product it gives.

clue.text: What one lacking drive might need to move forwards?

definitions.text: What one lacking drive might need to move forwards

parts.note: the surface offers a person with no motivation, someone who cannot get going; read it of a vehicle and 'drive' is the engine's power reaching the wheels
for the idle person this would be a pep talk; for the dead car it has to be a physical link to something in front that is still moving

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to find here. Both halves of the sentence read twice over, and the answer is the object that makes the second reading true.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue describes the thing itself: a car with no power of its own is pulled along by a line fastened to the vehicle ahead.

clue.text: Discrimination — is blame misdirected?

indicators.note: Something misdirected has been sent the wrong way, so the letters end up somewhere other than where they started.

parts.note: seven letters handed straight over from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks whether fault is being aimed at the wrong people, which sits very close to what the answer itself describes. That is neat setting, not coincidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Discrimination -> ABLEISM: ableism is prejudice against disabled people, one named form of discrimination, so the general word defines it by category.

clue.text: They take temporary charge of toilets

parts.note: re means about or concerning, the two letters a memo heading uses for 'of'
in Britain the men's public lavatory is signed the Gents

explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' is not joinery here but a piece of the build, which is what lets the definition stop dead at 'charge' with the sentence still reading smoothly.
explanation.definitionFit: They take temporary charge -> REGENTS: a regent rules in place of a monarch who is absent, ill or under age, and only until that ends.

clue.text: Maybe hoovers furniture top to bottom

indicators.note: In a down entry the first letter is the one at the top, and this sends it all the way round to the far end.

parts.note: a seat is a piece of furniture

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain any vacuum cleaner is a hoover, and to hoover food is to clear it fast and greedily. That slang sense is what the definition leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Maybe hoovers -> EATS: to hoover food is to eat it greedily, one particular way of eating, which is what the 'maybe' concedes.

clue.text: Irish city's workers take indirect route?

parts.note: Cork is a city and county in the south of Ireland
the possessive apostrophe-s hands over its own letter
a crew is a body of workers, on a ship or a film set

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb, which is easy to miss when the answer is such a familiar noun. The question mark marks the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: take indirect route -> CORKSCREW: to corkscrew is to move in a twisting spiral rather than straight on, the path the tool's own thread follows.

clue.text: Reasonable to run away

definitions.meaning: the slang clipping of legitimate: above board, within the rules, nothing to answer for
split the five letters after the third and you have the British phrase for taking to your heels

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the disguise: (5) hides the fact that the second definition wants the letters read as two words rather than one.
explanation.definitionFit: Reasonable -> LEGIT: slang for legitimate, so above board; and 'to run away' is leg it, the same five letters split after the third.

clue.text: Monkey bars cut down, abuse received

indicators.note: A word cut down is shortened, and it is the tail end that goes.
What is received is taken in, so the jeer goes inside the other piece instead of alongside it.

parts.note: to bar something is to ban it
a boo is the noise a crowd throws at a performer it wants to abuse

explanation.walkthrough: 'Monkey bars' is the trap: it reads as the playground climbing frame, but the definition stops after one word and 'bars' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkey -> BABOON: a baboon is a large ground-dwelling African monkey, so the general word defines it by example.

clue.text: Football team without wingers got grief and, ultimately, lost

indicators.note: Wingers play out on the flanks, so a word without them loses the letter at each edge and keeps the middle.

parts.note: the middle letter, once the outer pair is dropped
the middle three, on the same instruction
the middle letter again, from a three-letter word

indicators.note: What happens ultimately happens at the very end, so only the final letter is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of that word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Without wingers' looks like a note on the team's formation. It is the instruction, and it is applied to three ordinary words in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Football team -> ORIENT: Orient is what everyone calls Leyton Orient, a London league club, so one team stands for the general phrase.

clue.text: Conservative affected by wind when speaking

indicators.note: Said out loud rather than written down, so what you want is the sound of the word and not its spelling.

parts.note: what the wind has done to something is blown it, and the past tense of blow is the word you say aloud

explanation.walkthrough: A homophone this short lives on its surface, and 'affected by wind' reads as a sail, a tree or a bad dinner long before it reads as a past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Conservative -> BLUE: blue is the British Conservative party's colour, as red is Labour's, so the party name stands in for the shade.

clue.text: Leather eye protector

definitions.meaning: the verb sense: to leather someone is to thrash them with a strap
the noun sense, and only half a word of it: the fringe of hair on the lid that keeps dust out

explanation.walkthrough: Four words, no wordplay, and the two definitions are different parts of speech: a verb for beating and a noun for hair. Both readings are ordinary English.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather -> LASH: to leather someone is to whip them, which is to lash; and an eyelash is the hair fringing the lid that shields the eye.

clue.text: He wrote "ladlecum", "enkoopia", "attery" and "runcible" originally

indicators.note: What a word was originally is what it began as, so only the opening character of each is wanted.

parts.note: the opening letter of the first invented word
the opening letter of the second
the opening letter of the third, which describes a squash in one of the nonsense poems
the opening letter of the fourth, the best known of them, as in the runcible spoon

explanation.walkthrough: All four are Edward Lear's own coinages, and several of the creatures from his poem The Quangle Wangle's Hat are hiding elsewhere in this grid.
explanation.definitionFit: He wrote -> LEAR: Edward Lear invented every one of these words in his nonsense verse, so the man is defined as the one who put them on paper.

clue.text: Covers removed from that end for fast bowler?

indicators.note: The covers of a word are the letters at either edge, so taking them off leaves only what was in the middle.
The end of a word is its final letter, and that is all of it that comes across.

parts.note: the two letters in the middle, once the outer pair goes
the final letter of that word

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cricket ground with the covers coming off before a quick bowler runs in. A bowler is also headgear, and this puzzle is built round a Lear poem with one in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: bowler -> HAT: a bowler is a stiff round-crowned hat, so the answer is defined by one example of it, which the question mark flags.

clue.text: Some revolting eyesore that's attached to the ceiling

indicators.note: Only part of what follows is wanted, and it is a part that runs straight through the words as they stand.
Something revolting turns, and here it is the letters that turn: read them back the way they came.

parts.note: four consecutive letters sitting in the middle of that word, printed the wrong way round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some revolting eyesore' reads as one phrase about something ugly. It is two separate instructions and a word to take the letters from.
explanation.definitionFit: attached to the ceiling -> ROSE: the ceiling rose is the round moulded plate fixed overhead that a light fitting hangs down from.

clue.text: Sports equipment? Inside — ask Ingrid

indicators.note: What you want is not the words themselves but something sitting within them, unbroken and in the order printed.

parts.note: three consecutive letters straddling the gap between those two words

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits this is one piece of equipment out of thousands, and the dash is punctuation the wordplay has no use for at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports equipment -> SKI: a ski is one of the pair strapped to your boots for downhill or cross-country racing, so the phrase covers it by example.

clue.text: Writer left to tour huge wine region

indicators.note: A tour goes round the outside of a place, so the letters named first wrap themselves about the ones named next.

parts.note: the person writing the clue is the setter, and setters refer to themselves this way
l is the standard abbreviation for left
os is outsize, the clothing label for the largest size

explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' as the setter talking about himself is a convention worth memorising: it turns up whenever a clue seems to need an author nobody can name.
explanation.definitionFit: wine region -> MOSEL: the Mosel is the German river valley whose steep slate slopes grow Riesling, spelled Moselle when the wine is sold in French.

clue.text: Solicitor covering face in public

indicators.note: A covered face cannot be seen, so the letter at the front of the word is hidden from the answer.

parts.note: a tout solicits custom in the street, selling tickets at inflated prices near the ground

explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts a lawyer in a mask in a crowd. A tout is the British street seller who solicits, and the definition is the sense of open knowledge.
explanation.definitionFit: in public -> OUT: when something is out it is public knowledge, the sense of 'the secret is out' rather than anything to do with leaving.

clue.text: Schedule has first couple returning on American vessel

indicators.note: The couple at the front are the opening two letters, and they are the only ones touched.
Letters that return come back the way they went, so that pair is written in the opposite order.

parts.note: a is the standard abbreviation for American
a rota is the schedule saying who is on duty and when

explanation.walkthrough: 'American vessel' promises a ship and the surface sails on. The vessel is anatomical, and 'American' has quietly been detached to give a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: vessel -> AORTA: the aorta is the great blood vessel leaving the heart, so this is the anatomical sense of the word, not the seagoing one.

clue.text: District using country club for grand social gathering

indicators.note: To use one thing in place of another is to swap it in, so what comes next takes over a spot already occupied.
This is the exchange rate: the piece named after it is the one that leaves, and the piece named before it moves in.

parts.note: a region is a district, an area marked off within a country
the United Nations is the club almost every country belongs to
g is the standard abbreviation for grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.walkthrough: The surface hires a country club for a big do. The phrase is really the club that countries join, and 'grand' is money rather than scale.
explanation.definitionFit: social gathering -> REUNION: a reunion is the party a family, class or regiment holds so that everyone can meet again after years apart.

clue.text: Agitated international seaman recalling difficulty

indicators.note: Agitate a mixture and everything in it is thrown about, so the letters do not come back in the order they went in.

parts.note: i is the standard abbreviation for international
six letters handed over as printed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalling' looks like an instruction to turn something round, sitting where an indicator would sit. Both words are the definition, and the only instruction is at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: recalling difficulty -> AMNESIA: amnesia is precisely a difficulty in recalling, the loss of memory that follows a blow, an illness or a shock.

clue.text: Fresh drink supplier opening late

indicators.note: A shop that opens late is shut when you get there, so its opening letter is not available to be used.

parts.note: a dairy supplies milk, and milk is a drink

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh drink' wants to be read as one phrase, a cold beer or a new round. The definition is the single word, and the wordplay starts at 'drink supplier'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh -> AIRY: an airy room is one with fresh air moving through it, so the adjective carries that sense of freshness rather than lightness.

clue.text: Revel topless, getting director excited

indicators.note: In a down entry the top is the first letter, and a topless word has lost exactly that.

parts.note: to carouse is to revel, drinking noisily and at length
d is the standard abbreviation for director

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a stripped-off party-goer and a delighted boss, and that picture is exactly what stops 'topless' looking like the instruction it is.
explanation.definitionFit: excited -> AROUSED: to be aroused is to be stirred up, the general sense of being excited into feeling or action rather than the sexual one.

clue.text: Worried Barking is relatively rough

indicators.note: In Britain barking means completely mad, and a word driven mad will not keep its letters in any settled order.

parts.note: seven letters handed over as printed

explanation.walkthrough: Barking is also a district of east London, which is what makes the capital letter look innocent. 'Relatively' is the quiet signal that the answer is a comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: relatively rough -> ROWDIER: rowdy means noisily rough, and 'relatively' asks for the comparative, so the answer is that adjective in its -er form.

clue.text: You once learnt he 'entertains' nurses

indicators.note: To nurse something is to hold it close and keep it safe, so these words are cradling the letters wanted.

parts.note: four consecutive letters running from the tail of the first word, through the second and into the third

explanation.walkthrough: 'Learnt he' has the ring of Bible English, matching the archaic answer so neatly that you stop seeing the letters running straight through it.
explanation.definitionFit: You once -> THEE: thee is the old object form of the singular you, kept alive in prayer and in northern speech, which is what 'once' dates.

clue.text: Brief time in hospital by Texan mission, holding strong

parts.note: h is the standard abbreviation for hospital, the letter on the road sign

indicators.note: Whatever holds something has it inside, so the letter named next goes within the word before it.

parts.note: the Alamo is the old Spanish mission at San Antonio, besieged in 1836
f is forte in music, the instruction to play strongly

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is British for 'wait a second', a spoken phrase rather than a word, which is why the enumeration comes in three odd little pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Brief time -> HALF A MO: a mo is a moment, so half of one is the shortest wait there is, as in 'hang on, I won't be long'.

clue.text: First half of specified number leave semi-public body

indicators.note: A word's first half is the letters up to its midpoint, and everything past that point is simply dropped.

parts.note: a quantity is a specified number or amount of something
to go is to leave

explanation.walkthrough: The word is an acronym — quasi-autonomous non-governmental organisation — and has been a staple of British political grumbling since the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: semi-public body -> QUANGO: a quango is set up and funded by government yet run at arm's length from it, so it is public and not public at once.

clue.text: Manipulate old laundry equipment, overturning the front

indicators.note: Stand the first letter on its head and it becomes a different letter altogether, and that new one is what you write.

parts.note: a mangle is the hand-cranked pair of rollers that squeezed the water out of the washing
an M stood on its head is a W

explanation.walkthrough: The instruction turns a letter over rather than a word, and only a few letters survive that treatment. M and W are the classic pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Manipulate -> WANGLE: to wangle something is to get it by contriving and finessing, which is manipulating a situation rather than an object.

clue.text: 'Moneybags' Nick admits personal hygiene problem

indicators.note: To admit someone is to let them in, so what follows goes inside the word named before it.

parts.note: to nab is to nick, in the sense of grabbing or pinching something
BO is body odour, the polite two letters for it

explanation.walkthrough: The word came home from India with the officials who made fortunes there, and it has meant conspicuous wealth ever since. The quotation marks flag the nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Moneybags -> NABOB: a nabob is a man of great and showy wealth, which is what calling someone moneybags accuses them of being.

clue.text: Tip from Chris Ramsey for youngster

indicators.note: The tip of a thing is its very point, and in a down entry that means the letter standing at the top.

parts.note: the first letter of that name
Alf Ramsey managed England to the World Cup in 1966

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chris Ramsey' reads as one person. The clue takes a letter from the first name and a famous football manager from the second.
explanation.definitionFit: youngster -> CALF: a calf is the young of the cow, so the general word for a young animal is defined by one particular instance.

clue.text: Poems most peculiar, but not every 3rd

indicators.note: Counting along the letters, each third one is passed over and the survivors are written down in the order they stood.

parts.note: the superlative of odd, six letters to count through

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'most peculiar' as an anagram signal. It is the fodder, and the only instruction in the clue comes after the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Poems -> ODES: an ode is a lyric poem addressed to its subject, a nightingale or a Grecian urn, and the plural matches the plural.

clue.text: Novelist's out of order

parts.note: Kingsley and his son Martin were both novelists of the first rank
the possessive apostrophe-s gives up its own letter

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as 'is' in the surface — the novelist is out of order — while the wordplay quietly takes the letter itself.
explanation.definitionFit: out of order -> AMISS: something amiss is wrong or not as it should be, the faulty sense of that phrase rather than the badly behaved one.

clue.text: Rower adlibs desperately going around in unfamiliar craft?

indicators.note: Someone acting desperately is following no plan at all, so the letters land in an order nobody chose.
What goes around a thing surrounds it, so the shuffled letters close over the piece named first.

parts.note: six letters handed over as printed, ready to be rearranged
an oar is the blade a rower pulls, so the word stands in for the person by naming their tool

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rower' looks like the person the surface is about. It is three letters standing for the thing they pull, which is the commonest way a setter hides a short word.
explanation.definitionFit: unfamiliar craft -> SAILBOARD: a sailboard is a floating board with a mast, a craft in the loosest sense and nothing an oarsman would recognise.

clue.text: Space to tuck into pudding, the 3rd for Jodie Marsh

indicators.note: To tuck in is to settle yourself inside something, so this piece goes within the word that follows it.

parts.note: a flan is a baked open tart, served as a pudding
an en is a printer's space, the width of the letter n

indicators.note: Count three letters into the name and stop; in a five-letter name that is the one standing in the middle.

parts.note: the third of that name's five letters

explanation.walkthrough: Jodie Marsh is a British media personality, so the two names read as one woman and hide the fact that only the first of them is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsh -> FENLAND: a fen is low waterlogged ground, so fenland is marshy country, of which the Fens of eastern England are the famous stretch.

clue.text: Strips of meat, good French cuts

indicators.note: Something that cuts into a thing goes right inside it, dividing the letters to make room for itself.

parts.note: ribs are a cut of meat, taken off the animal's side
bon is the French for good

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts' works twice over: in the surface it is a butcher's word sitting beside the meat, and in the wordplay it is the knife going in.
explanation.definitionFit: Strips -> RIBBONS: a ribbon is a long narrow strip of fabric, and 'torn to ribbons' is exactly torn to strips, so both are plural.
